_why: Proposed edits to data/courses/rocks-and-minerals-b-2027.json that close the Division B gaps found by comparing the 2027 Starter Pack with the live course. Lesson objects use the blueprint's own schema (slug, title, objective, keywords, high_weight, optional video). Every item names its authority in the 2027 Div B rules (rules_ref) and the pack slides and exam items that support it. No Division C topic is proposed: solid solution, phase diagrams, silicate-structure classes, crystal systems, metamorphic facies, magmatic differentiation and thin sections are listed under excluded. This is a proposal only. Nothing has been applied to the repo or the database.
_schema_note: new_lessons[].lesson is a drop-in lesson object for units[slug=unit].lessons, inserted after the lesson named in 'after'. changed_lessons[] gives replacement objective text (null = unchanged) and keywords to add or remove for an existing lesson slug.

lesson.title: Diaphaneity and Tenacity
lesson.objective: Classify a specimen as transparent, translucent or opaque, and describe its tenacity as brittle, malleable, sectile, flexible or elastic, using List examples: clear calcite (transparent), milky quartz (translucent), hematite (opaque); quartz (brittle), native copper (malleable), talc (sectile), mica (elastic).

new_lessons.why: Rule 3.h.iii lists both as physical properties. The live course never teaches diaphaneity as a property and has no tenacity content. The pack tests both.

lesson.title: Acid, Fluorescence, Magnetism and the Other Listed Properties
lesson.objective: Name the eight 'other properties' the rules allow (reaction with acid, fluorescence, magnetism, smell, taste, double refraction, piezoelectricity, radioactivity), give a List example for each where one exists (calcite vs dolomite in acid, fluorite and willemite under UV, magnetite, sulfur odor, halite taste, calcite double refraction, quartz piezoelectricity), and interpret a written description of an acid or taste result, since HCl is never provided and tasting is never allowed.

new_lessons.why: Rule 3.h.iv lists exactly these eight properties. Smell, taste, double refraction, piezoelectricity and radioactivity have zero hits in the live course. The pack gives the examples. Do NOT carry over slide 20's 'sulfur smells like rotten eggs' (see pack_audit.md). The pack's radioactive examples (uraninite, autunite) are not on the List, so the lesson must say no List mineral is a standard radioactivity example rather than invent one.

lesson.title: Mineral Habits: The 21 Listed Forms
lesson.objective: Recognize and name all 21 habits the rules list (acicular, bladed, botryoidal, cubic, dendritic, dodecahedral, doubly terminated, druzy, geodic, hexagonal, hopper, massive, micaceous, octahedral, pisolitic, prismatic, radiating, rosette, stalactitic, twinning, tabular) from a description or photo, and give a List mineral that shows each where one is standard, such as pyrite cubes, botryoidal malachite, dendritic silver, micaceous muscovite, tabular barite.

new_lessons.why: Rule 3.h.v gives a closed list of 21 habits. Eight of them have zero hits in the live course. The pack's slide 22 is titled 'Full 2027 List' but omits twinning and tabular, so build from the rules, not the slide. Habit is tested 7 times across the three Div B pack exams.

lesson.title: Formulas, Trace-Element Color and Polymorphs
lesson.objective: Read a mineral formula, explain how a trace element changes color without changing the mineral (chromium in emerald, iron in amethyst), and identify the four polymorph sets the rules name — aragonite/calcite (CaCO3), diamond/graphite (C), orthoclase/microcline (KAlSi3O8), andalusite/kyanite/sillimanite (Al2SiO5) — stating why the same formula can give different properties.

new_lessons.why: Rules 3.h.vi and 3.h.vii. 'Polymorph' appears once in the live course and andalusite never appears. The pack tests polymorphs or trace-element color in 5 Div B items and 3 Div C items.

lesson.title: How and Where Minerals Form
lesson.objective: Match each rules-listed formation process to a List example: crystallization from magma (olivine in basalt, feldspar in granite), hydrothermal (quartz veins, galena, fluorite), chemical weathering (feldspar to kaolinite), evaporites (halite, gypsum), chemical precipitation (travertine calcite), alteration under heat and pressure (garnet, kyanite, staurolite). Then link minerals to rock-forming settings: mafic olivine and pyroxene in oceanic crust, evaporite minerals in sedimentary basins, metamorphic minerals in regional belts.

new_lessons.why: Rules 3.h.x and 3.h.xi. 'Hydrothermal' and 'chemical weathering' have zero hits in the lessons. Nothing links minerals to settings.

lesson.title: Uses of Minerals and Rocks
lesson.objective: State an accurate economic use for common List minerals and rocks: hematite and banded iron formation as iron ore, galena as lead ore, gypsum for drywall and plaster, fluorite as a steelmaking flux and fluorine source, corundum as an abrasive and gem, quartz for glass and piezoelectric timing, halite for salt and chemicals, zircon for geochronology, graphite for pencils and lubricants; granite, marble, slate and sandstone as building stone; limestone as agricultural lime; coal as fuel.

new_lessons.why: Rules 3.h.xiii.1 and 3.i.viii. The live course has no uses content at all: 'ore of', geochronology, drywall and electronics each have zero hits. It is the most-tested missing topic in the pack, with 12+ items. Every listed use is stated in a pack slide or answer key.

lesson.title: Batholiths, Lava Flows, Pyroclastic Deposits and Plate Boundaries
lesson.objective: Describe the three igneous formations the rules allow (batholith, lava flow, pyroclastic deposit) and the textures they produce (phaneritic, aphanitic/glassy/vesicular, pyroclastic), explain pegmatitic texture, and predict the igneous rock typical of each plate setting: basalt at mid-ocean ridges, andesite and diorite at subduction zones, granite at continental convergent boundaries.

new_lessons.why: Rules 3.i.iv.1, 3.i.iv.3 and 3.i.iv.5. Batholith, lava flow, pyroclastic, mid-ocean ridge and subduction all have zero hits in the live course. Keep laccolith OUT: slide 39 teaches it and B-State Q21 tests it, but rule 3.i.iv.3 limits formations to the three named.

lesson.title: Grain Size, Sorting, Rounding and Environments of Deposition
lesson.objective: Order the grain sizes clay < silt < sand < pebble < cobble < boulder and relate size to the water or wind velocity needed to move them. Use sorting and rounding to infer transport distance and energy. Match the ten rules-named environments (alluvial fan, delta, fluvial, lacustrine, swamp, aeolian, floodplain, beach, shallow marine/shelf, deep marine) to their typical sediment, recognizing alluvial fans as high-energy, poorly sorted and angular.

new_lessons.why: Rules 3.i.v.3–5. 'Energy' and 'velocity' have zero hits, and 3 of the 10 environments are never named. This is heavily tested in the pack. Build from slide 43 and the exam keys, NOT slide 60, which wrongly calls alluvial fans low-energy.

lesson.title: Primary Sedimentary Structures
lesson.objective: Identify plane bedding, cross-bedding, ripple marks, mud cracks, graded bedding, and fossil tracks and trails from a description or photo, and state what each implies about the depositional process: current or wind direction, drying and exposure, waning-energy events, or organisms active on soft sediment.

new_lessons.why: Rule 3.i.v.6. The live course has zero content on primary sedimentary structures. The pack tests them 7 times, including with photos (cross-bedding).

changed_lessons.objective: Distinguish a mineral from a rock using the rules' definitions — a mineral is a naturally occurring, inorganic, solid substance with a definite composition and crystalline structure; a rock is a naturally occurring solid mass of one mineral (monomineralic, e.g. quartzite) or several (polymineralic, e.g. granite), or of mineraloid or organic matter (e.g. coal) — and justify the distinction with evidence.
changed_lessons.why: The rules' definitions (3.h.i, 3.i.i) include 'solid' and the mono/polymineralic distinction. The live lesson omits both. The expert review flagged the missing 'solid' and it is still unfixed live.

changed_lessons.objective: Use the Mohs index minerals (gypsum 2, calcite 3, fluorite 4, apatite 5, orthoclase 6, quartz 7) and a glass plate (about 5.5) and streak plate (about 6.5–7) as comparison surfaces, and bracket an unknown's hardness between supported values.
changed_lessons.why: The live lesson uses dioptase and chalcopyrite as references and gives gypsum as 1.5–2. The Mohs index mineral defines 2 (slide 9). The pack's B-National Q30 relies on glass ≈5.5, and slide 11 gives the streak plate as ~6.5. The fingernail and copper values the title promises are not in the pack; source them separately.

changed_lessons.objective: Classify igneous rocks as felsic, intermediate, mafic or ultramafic from silica content and minerals. Trace Bowen's Reaction Series: discontinuous olivine → pyroxene → amphibole → biotite and continuous Ca-rich → Na-rich plagioclase, converging to K-feldspar → muscovite → quartz. Explain why early, high-temperature minerals such as olivine weather fastest at Earth's surface and quartz resists weathering.
changed_lessons.why: The rules say 'felsic' (3.i.iv.2). The live lesson teaches 'silicic', omits the full discontinuous sequence and K-feldspar → muscovite → quartz, and never states the weathering corollary, which the pack tests in three exams. Use the exam diagram (Image 5/8/10), not slide 31, which draws the final three minerals side by side.
Rule 3.i.iv.1 lists seven textures. The live lesson teaches five; pyroclastic and pegmatitic have zero hits.

The objective already names pumice, syenite, pegmatite and tuff breccia, but the live text never teaches them. Tuff breccia is one of the 8 unnamed specimens. Adding the keywords steers passage selection toward texture evidence: pumice is light and vesicular, scoria dark and vesicular (slide 60); tuff and tuff breccia are pyroclastic (slide 37).

changed_lessons.objective: Distinguish plagioclase from potassium feldspar by cleavage angle and striations, and identify albite, labradorite, amazonite and orthoclase/microcline (the pink/tan potassium feldspar). Separate pyroxenes (augite; two cleavages near 90°) from amphiboles (hornblende, actinolite, tremolite; cleavages near 60°/120°). Name the feldspar, pyroxene and amphibole groups as the List does, including rhodonite and spodumene in the Pyroxene Group, and sodalite.
changed_lessons.why: Augite has zero hits in the live course. The List places augite, rhodonite and spodumene in the Pyroxene Group; the pack's slide 29 omits rhodonite, so use the List. The pack gives augite's group, dark color and ~90° cleavage.

The title promises beryl and tourmaline, but the live text names each only once. The pack gives: tourmaline is a complex boron silicate, piezoelectric and color-zoned, and 'Tourmaline' alone is accepted for ID (List note 3). Beryl is the mineral behind emerald, aquamarine and morganite. Chrysocolla is also named in the objective and is absent from the text.

Celestite/Celestine and Turquoise are 2 of the 8 unnamed specimens. The pack confirms celestite is a sulfate (slide 57) and turquoise is a phosphate, blue-green and massive, used as a gemstone and ornamental material (slide 57; C-State Q25–26). The pack gives no identifying properties for celestite, so source those independently.

Aventurine (one of the 8 unnamed) is on the List as a quartz variety (slide 58), but the pack gives no properties for it, so they must be sourced independently. The List files Opal under Quartz varieties; the pack moves it to 'Individual Silicates'. Teach that the List groups opal with the quartz varieties while it is an amorphous mineraloid.

Rule 3.i.vi.1 names slaty cleavage, schistose and banding. 'Slaty cleavage' and 'gneissic banding' have zero hits live. Slide 45 ties them to low, medium and high grade. Note: gneissic banding is COARSE; slide 60's 'fine banding' is wrong.

changed_lessons.objective: Order the seven index minerals the rules list — chlorite, muscovite, biotite (low grade); garnet, staurolite (medium); kyanite, sillimanite (high) — explain what an index mineral tells you about grade, and distinguish contact from regional metamorphism by scale and dominant agent.
changed_lessons.why: The live lesson says muscovite is 'not a single step' in the sequence. That is true of the Barrovian zones, but it contradicts the rules, which list muscovite among the 7 index minerals (3.i.vi.6), and the pack's order chlorite → muscovite → biotite (slide 46). Students must be able to answer a rules-framed question. The Barrovian nuance can stay as a note.

Rule 3.i.vii names 'melting & solidification; uplift, erosion & deposition; burial, compaction & cementation; heat & pressure resulting in recrystallization & deformation'. 'Uplift' has zero hits live.

excluded_div_c.topic: Phase diagram interpretation (T/P, T/X, feldspar ternary)
Magmatic differentiation (fractional crystallization, assimilation, magma mixing)
Thin sections and photomicrographs (Div C, State/National)
Laccolith (outside the Div B list of igneous formations)
